section.title: The Resurrection
section.sectionRationale: At dawn on the first day of the week the women come with spices and find the stone rolled away and the tomb empty. Two men in radiant apparel ask why they seek the living among the dead and declare that He has risen, reminding them of Jesus' own words in Galilee. The women remember, and run to tell the Eleven, who dismiss it as nonsense, though Peter runs to the tomb and goes away wondering. The resurrection dawns quietly, on the word of angels and the memory of Jesus' promise.
section.thesis: Jesus is risen exactly as He said, so the empty tomb is not a riddle but the fulfillment of His own word, calling His people to stop seeking the living among the dead and to remember and believe what He foretold.
section.frameNote: Two movements: the women at the empty tomb and the angels' announcement; and the report to the Eleven with Peter running to see.

units.label: The empty tomb and the angels' word
units.note: why do you look for the living among the dead

verses.text: On the first day of the week, very early in the morning, the women came to the tomb, bringing the spices they had prepared.
They found the stone rolled away from the tomb,
but when they entered, they did not find the body of the Lord Jesus.
While they were puzzling over this, suddenly two men in radiant apparel stood beside them.
As the women bowed their faces to the ground in terror, the two men asked them, “Why do you look for the {{zao|living}} among the dead?
He is not here; He has {{egeiro|risen}}! Remember how He told you while He was still in Galilee:
‘The Son of Man {{dei|must}} be delivered into the hands of sinful men, and be crucified, and on the third day rise again.’”
And when they returned from the tomb, they reported all these things to the Eleven and to all the others.
It was Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James, and the other women with them who told this to the apostles.
But their words seemed like nonsense to them, and they did not believe the women.
Peter, however, got up and ran to the tomb. And after bending down and seeing only the linen cloths, he went away, wondering to himself what had happened.

zao.gloss: To live, to be alive. The angels' question, why do you look for the living among the dead, announces that Jesus belongs no longer among the dead but among the living. He is the Living One, death behind Him, and the tomb is empty because life has conquered.

egeiro.gloss: To raise up, to rouse from sleep or death. He has been raised, the angels declare, the passive pointing to the Father who raised His Son. The resurrection is God's mighty act of vindication, reversing the verdict of the cross and inaugurating the new creation.

dei.gloss: It is necessary, it must be. The Son of Man must be delivered, crucified, and rise, a divine necessity fixed in God's plan and foretold in Scripture. The cross and resurrection were no accident but the appointed way of salvation, exactly as Jesus had said.

mimnesko.gloss: To remember, to call to mind. The angels do not offer new information but recall Jesus' own words, and the women remember. Faith in the resurrection is grounded in remembering what Jesus foretold; His word interprets the empty tomb.

basic.context: Very early on Sunday, the women who had watched Jesus die come to the tomb with spices to finish His burial. They find the stone rolled away and the body gone. As they stand bewildered, two men in dazzling clothes appear and ask why they are seeking the living among the dead. He is not here, they say, He has risen, and they remind the women of what Jesus taught in Galilee: that the Son of Man must be crucified and on the third day rise. The women remember His words and hurry back to tell the Eleven and the others. But the report sounds like nonsense to the apostles, and they do not believe. Only Peter runs to the tomb, sees the empty linen cloths, and goes away wondering what has happened.
basic.hermeneutics: Luke grounds the resurrection not in speculation but in the word of Jesus recalled by the angels. The empty tomb is interpreted by His prior teaching: this had to happen, and He said it would. The disbelief of the apostles underlines that faith comes by remembering and trusting His word, not by natural expectation.
basic.originalLanguages: The angels ask why they seek the zao, the living, among the dead, for Jesus has egeiro, been raised. This happened because the Son of Man dei, must, suffer and rise, a divine necessity. And faith begins as the women mimnesko, remember, His words.
basic.typology: The third-day rising fulfills the pattern of Jonah and the promise of Scripture. The first day of the week becomes the day of new creation, the dawn of God's new world in the risen Christ. The women as first witnesses fulfill the reversal by which God chooses the lowly to proclaim His greatest deed.
basic.christ: Jesus is the Living One who has conquered death, raised by the Father exactly as He foretold. He is the Son of Man whose suffering and rising were a divine necessity written in Scripture, and the risen Lord whose own word is the key that unlocks the meaning of the empty tomb.
basic.god: God is the one who raised Jesus, vindicating His Son and reversing the cross. He keeps His word to the letter, so that what Jesus promised has come to pass. He chooses faithful women as the first heralds of the resurrection, honoring the lowly and the overlooked.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 15 lists the resurrection appearances and calls it of first importance. Luke 9 records Jesus foretelling His death and rising. Psalm 16 promises that God will not let His Holy One see decay. Acts 2 preaches that God raised Jesus, freeing Him from the pangs of death.
basic.oneStory: The tomb is empty because the crucified King is alive, raised as He said. The story that ran through the cross now breaks into dawn, and the first word of the new creation is an invitation to remember Jesus' promise and believe, to stop seeking the living among the dead.

context.literary:
Luke 24 is the hinge of the whole two part work Luke wrote. It closes the Gospel and, as Luke 24:44 to 49 and Acts 1:1 to 8 show, it hands the story on to the book of Acts. Within the chapter, verses 1 to 12 open a single day, the first day of the week, that will not end until verse 49. Everything here is a first movement: the discovery, the interpretation, the report, the refusal to believe, and one man's puzzled run.

The scene is built in three beats. First comes what the women see: the stone rolled away, the empty place, and no body, verses 1 to 3. Luke lets the bare facts stand with no explanation. Then comes what they hear, verses 4 to 7. The two men do not argue; they ask a question and then press a memory. The emptiness is interpreted only by the word Jesus had already spoken. Third comes what happens to the witness, verses 8 to 12. The women remember, they tell, they are dismissed, and Peter goes to see for himself.

Notice how heavily Luke leans on verbs of seeing, finding and not finding. The women 'found' the stone, 'did not find' the body, and Peter sees 'only' the linen cloths.

The women are named only at the end, in verse 10, after their message has already been told. Luke also builds a chain of contrasts: women who believe and apostles who do not, a rejected report and a confirmed one, terror in verse 5 and wondering in verse 12. The passage ends with an open question, 'what had happened', that the rest of the chapter exists to answer.
context.historical:
Luke has been preparing this scene since Luke 23:50 to 56. Joseph of Arimathea laid the body in a rock cut tomb 'where no one had yet been laid,' Luke 23:53, and the women 'saw the tomb and how His body was placed,' Luke 23:55. They then went home and 'rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment,' Luke 23:56. That is why they do not come until the first day of the week. The burial on Friday had been rushed because the Sabbath was beginning, Luke 23:54, so the spices and perfumes were an act of devotion left unfinished.

A tomb of this kind was a chamber cut into rock and closed by a large stone, often one that rolled in a groove across the entrance. The women's worry about moving it is stated in Mark 16:3. Luke omits the worry and tells only the result: the stone is already rolled away.

Women were the natural people to tend a body, so their presence at the tomb is entirely ordinary. Luke had introduced them long before. Luke 8:2 to 3 names 'Mary called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out' and 'Joanna the wife of Herod's household manager Chuza' among the women who supported Jesus 'out of their own means,' and Luke 23:55 calls them the women who had come with Him from Galilee. The Eleven are 'the Eleven' because Judas is gone; the number itself is a reminder of failure.

The apostles' reaction reflects how a report like this would have been heard. Nothing in the ordinary Jewish expectation looked for one man to rise ahead of everyone else. The hope was for a general resurrection at the end of the age, Daniel 12:2 and John 11:24. A single resurrection in the middle of history, in a tomb in Jerusalem, had no category waiting for it, which helps explain why the Eleven take it for foolish talk in verse 11 and why Luke does not hide that.
context.canonical:
The chapter looks back before it looks forward. The angels' appeal to what Jesus said in Galilee reaches to Luke 9:22, 9:44 and 18:31 to 33, where He spoke of being delivered up and of rising on the third day, and where He said that 'everything the prophets have written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled.' Luke 24 is the collecting of those promissory notes. Behind the third day stand the patterns of Scripture itself: Hosea 6:2, 'on the third day He will raise us up,' Genesis 22:4 where Isaac is received back on the third day, and Jonah's three days in the fish, Matthew 12:40. Paul's summary in 1 Corinthians 15:3 to 4 is that Christ was raised on the third day 'according to the Scriptures,' meaning that the pattern, not a single proof text, carries the argument.

Psalm 16:10, 'nor will You let Your Holy One see decay,' is taken by Peter in Acts 2:24 to 32 to be fulfilled in the resurrection, and Daniel 7:13 to 14 shows the Son of Man receiving dominion after being brought into the presence of God, which is the vindication this chapter announces.

The passage is also the opening of the church's calendar. The first day of the week became the day of gathering, Acts 20:7, because it was the day Christ rose. And the chapter is the gate to Acts: the same Luke who ends with an empty tomb begins Acts 1:3 with the claim that Jesus 'presented Himself to them with many convincing proofs that He was alive.' Paul lists those appearances in 1 Corinthians 15:5 to 8, beginning, as Luke 24:34 will, with Cephas.

All four Gospels place women at the tomb, Matthew 28:1 to 10, Mark 16:1 to 8 and John 20:1 to 18, with differing details. The agreement on the women is the strongest thing they share.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke wrote so that Theophilus might 'know the certainty of the things you have been taught,' Luke 1:4, and the empty tomb is the hardest of those things to hold. He does not try to prove it by argument. He tells it as it was received, including the unflattering parts. The first witnesses are not the Twelve but women whose word the Twelve brush aside, and the apostle most often on stage, Peter, arrives only to see cloths and go home puzzled. A writer inventing the story for credit would not have designed it this way.

What Luke wants his readers to take from it is that the resurrection is not a bolt from the blue but the keeping of a promise. The angels do not say 'Look, a miracle.' They say 'Remember how He told you.' The scene is arranged so that the reader, like the women, is sent back to the earlier chapters to see that Jesus had said all this plainly, and that the unbelief of the Eleven was a failure of memory more than a failure of evidence.

Luke also means his hearers to share the women's movement from terror to remembering to telling. He expects the faith of the reader to have the same shape: hear the word, recall what the Lord said, and bear witness, even when the report is not welcomed.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes what happened on one morning. It does not command that anyone must go to a tomb, hold dawn services or reproduce the women's spices. The few imperatives are the angels' 'Remember' in verse 6 and the implied call to stop looking for the living among the dead. Those carry across the centuries, because they address the habit of seeking the Lord in the wrong place, in what is past and lifeless, rather than in the risen Christ who is present by His word.

It also describes the unbelief of the apostles without endorsing it. Luke reports their reaction honestly, and the fact that they doubted does not make doubt a virtue. At the same time the text does not scold the women for weeping or the apostles for needing to see; it simply shows the Lord leading them out of that, as the next scenes do. The right use of this account is to take courage when our own report of Christ is dismissed, and to let Jesus' words, rather than our expectations, set what we think is possible.

debates.question: What kind of resurrection does the empty tomb announce?

views.label: A bodily raising of the same Jesus
views.case: The empty tomb, the missing body in verse 3 and the linen cloths left behind in verse 12 only make sense if the body that was buried is the body that was raised. Luke goes on in verses 39 to 43 to have Jesus eat and be touched, and Paul lists the resurrection with a burial first, 1 Corinthians 15:4. This has been the church's settled reading from the start.

views.label: A spiritual or visionary resurrection, with the tomb story as later legend
views.case: Some argue that the earliest faith arose from visions of the risen Lord and that the empty tomb was added later to give them a physical anchor. They point to the fact that Paul never mentions the tomb in 1 Corinthians 15.

views.label: A transformed physical body, not a resuscitation
views.case: Others hold that the tomb really was empty but that what was raised was not the old body restored to its old life, as with Lazarus, John 11:44, but that body made new, which Paul calls 'a spiritual body,' 1 Corinthians 15:44, one that is bodily yet no longer bound by death.

debates.bearing: Luke leaves no room for a purely inward resurrection. The empty tomb, the cloths, the Lord's flesh and bones in verse 39 and the shared meal all insist on a real body. Paul's 'burial' in 1 Corinthians 15:4 assumes the same thing: a buried body that rose. The third view guards a point Luke also makes, that this is not simply Lazarus revived, since the risen Jesus comes and goes in ways no ordinary body does.

debates.question: How should the different Gospel accounts of the angels at the tomb be handled?

views.label: Harmonise them as complementary reports
views.case: Luke has two men, Matthew one angel, Mark a young man and John two angels. This view holds that each writer selects. A report of one does not deny the presence of a second, and the women may have come and gone in groups, since Luke 24:10 names several women. On this view nothing needs to be corrected.

views.label: Treat them as independent testimony with differences in detail
views.case: Others say these differences are what one expects when several witnesses recall a startling event, and that real agreement on the core, the tomb, the women, the message that He has risen, is more convincing for not being tidied. They do not think a perfect harmony can or should be forced.

debates.bearing: Both views hold that the central claim is unaffected. Every Gospel has the tomb empty, the women first, and a heavenly message. Luke's own care shows in his sequel: in Acts 1:10 he again uses 'two men dressed in white,' so his language of two men is a considered way of speaking of angels, not a slip.

study.originalLanguages:
Several of Luke's choices in these twelve verses repay slow reading, beyond the words the study already marks.

Verse 1 puts the time in a way English hides. Luke writes literally 'on the first of the Sabbaths,' as the BSB footnote notes, an idiom for the first day of the Sabbath week, and he adds that it was 'very early in the morning,' which renders a phrase meaning something like 'deep dawn.' The women arrive while it is still barely light.

In verse 4 the men's clothing is 'radiant,' from a verb related to lightning. Luke uses the same family of words in Luke 17:24 of lightning flashing from one end of the sky to the other. The image is of brilliance that flashes. The same verse says they 'stood beside' the women, a verb Luke often uses for sudden heavenly appearances.

In verse 5 the women 'bowed their faces to the ground,' a natural reaction in the presence of the divine. The men's question, 'Why do you look for the living among the dead?', uses a plural 'you,' and the verb 'look for' is a present tense, so it carries the sense 'why do you keep on seeking.' The question is gentle correction of a continuing habit.

Verse 7 gives the angels' summary of the Galilee teaching, and the verb for 'rise again' is a different one from the passive 'He has risen' in verse 6. The first is active, 'to stand up,' the second is passive, 'He was raised.' Between them, Luke lets both truths stand: He was raised by the Father and He rose. Peter will later preach that 'God raised Him from the dead,' Acts 2:24, and the Gospel record does not feel any tension in saying both.

In verse 11 the apostles' response is that the women's words 'seemed like nonsense.' The Greek is a strong word for idle talk, the kind of thing said by someone raving. And the verb 'did not believe' is in the imperfect tense, 'they kept refusing to believe,' not a single reaction but a settled stance. Luke uses the same verb of the disciples again in verse 41, where it is joy that holds them back.

In verse 12 Peter 'wondering to himself' translates a verb of amazement used for the astonishment of the crowds at miracles, Luke 4:22 and 8:25. It is neither belief nor denial, but a mind caught in the middle. A note on the manuscripts: this verse is absent from a few ancient copies, but it stands in the great majority, and Luke 24:24 presupposes it when it says that 'some of our companions went to the tomb.'

typology.type: The third day, Genesis 22:4 and Jonah
typology.fulfillment: Abraham reached Moriah on the third day, and in 'a sense he did receive Isaac back from death,' Hebrews 11:19. Jonah came out of the fish after three days and nights, which Jesus calls the sign of the Son of Man, Matthew 12:40. Hosea 6:2 speaks of being raised up on the third day. In Christ these scattered third days become one event: the beloved Son who was truly offered, truly died, and truly rose. The type falls short because Isaac was spared at the last moment and Jonah did not die, while Jesus actually died and was raised. Paul says all this happened 'according to the Scriptures,' 1 Corinthians 15:4.

typology.type: The first day of the week, Genesis 1:5
typology.fulfillment: Genesis 1 numbers the days and ends the first with the words 'the first day.' On the first day God spoke light into the dark, Genesis 1:3. Luke places the resurrection at dawn on the first day of the week, Luke 24:1. John adds that it was 'still dark,' John 20:1. The correspondence is that a new creation begins where the old one began, with light after dark, which is why Paul can call the risen Christ 'the firstfruits,' 1 Corinthians 15:20, and the church gathered on this day, Acts 20:7. The text does not call it a new creation outright, so the link is an inference, but one that the later writers invite, 2 Corinthians 5:17.

Isaiah said the Servant 'was assigned a grave with the wicked, and with a rich man in His death.' Luke tells how Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the council who had not agreed with the others, begged for the body and laid it in a new tomb, Luke 23:50 to 53. The burial the prophet described was exactly what happened, which makes the empty tomb the second half of the same prophecy: after the anguish, 'He will see the light of life,' Isaiah 53:11. The type is not a ritual but a prediction, and it is exceeded in that the Servant not only dies in the wrong company but rises.

typology.type: The Son of Man vindicated, Daniel 7:13 to 14
typology.fulfillment: Daniel sees 'One like the Son of Man' brought before the Ancient of Days and given 'dominion, glory, and kingship.' Jesus uses 'the Son of Man' as His own title, and the angels use it in verse 7 for the one who must be delivered, crucified and rise. The pattern is that the Son of Man suffers and is then vindicated by God. The resurrection is the first public step of that vindication, and Acts 2:33 says He was then exalted to the right hand of God. Daniel's vision falls short of the cross, since it shows the glory and not the cost, which Jesus supplies.

study.christ:
The passage leads to Christ through His own words. Almost everything the angels say is a quotation of something Jesus had already said, so the first Easter sermon is preached by the Lord Himself long before the event. He had told the disciples that the Son of Man must be delivered, crucified and rise, Luke 9:22, and that 'everything the prophets have written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled,' Luke 18:31 to 33. The empty tomb shows that His word is reliable down to the day.

He is also the Son of Man of Daniel 7. Daniel sees One 'like the Son of Man' approach the Ancient of Days and receive 'dominion, glory, and kingship,' Daniel 7:13 to 14. The suffering of verse 7, 'sinful men,' and the rising are the gate into that vindication. Paul says that He 'was declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead,' Romans 1:4, not that He became Son then, but that the resurrection openly displays who He is.

He is the Lord of life in a deeper sense than the text of verse 5 first suggests. 'The living' stands against 'the dead,' and the question implies that the One they seek belongs to the living, which Revelation 1:18 states directly in His own mouth, where He calls Himself 'the Living One.' The verse shows what is at stake: if He is the living, then the grave is no longer the last word, and the burial spices become the last gesture of an old world.

He is the firstfruits. Paul calls Him 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,' 1 Corinthians 15:20. The empty tomb is not only His story but the first sheaf of a harvest, which is why believers are promised their own resurrection.

Care is needed here. Luke does not tell us how the resurrection occurred, and he does not describe it. The tomb is empty before anyone arrives, and the angels explain it by one fact: He has risen. The only dogma the text asks us to hold is that a real man who died a real death is alive again, as He said, and that this is the fulfillment of what He taught, not an addition to it.

Finally, He is the one who restores the failures. The Eleven who do not believe, and Peter who goes away wondering, will be met by Him in the rest of the chapter. The tomb is where Jesus' promise meets their failure, and the promise wins.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who acts first and explains second. The stone is moved and the body is gone before any person arrives, so the resurrection is God's own deed, not something produced by the women's faith or the apostles' expectation. The passive 'He has risen' in verse 6 points to the Father who raised the Son. Peter says exactly this: 'God raised Him from the dead, releasing Him from the agony of death, because it was impossible for Him to be held in its clutches,' Acts 2:24. God is not the bystander of the cross but its vindicator.

He is the God who keeps His word to the letter. The angels' whole argument is 'Remember how He told you.' What was spoken in Galilee comes true in Jerusalem on the third day, and it is consistent with what the prophets had been saying for centuries, Luke 18:31. Isaiah had said the same of His own word: 'it will accomplish what I please,' Isaiah 55:11. The empty tomb is that word coming true in the most unlikely place.

He is also the God who sends messengers. He does not leave the women to interpret an empty tomb for themselves. Two men in radiant clothing come and speak. God's way of dealing with confusion is to supply a word, not merely a sign, which is why the angels spend the whole scene reminding rather than showing.

He is a God who chooses the unlikely. The first witnesses are women who, in a world that rarely trusted them as formal witnesses, are given the news first. They include Mary Magdalene, whose story had begun with seven demons going out of her, Luke 8:2. The God who raised Jesus honors those whom people overlook, and He does not depend on the reaction of the powerful.

He is patient with unbelief. The apostles dismiss the report as nonsense, and Peter only wonders, yet no rebuke is recorded here. God moves them forward, one scene at a time, until the whole group is gathered in verse 33 and says 'The Lord has indeed risen.'

For worship, this means that praise to the God who raises the dead is not a matter of sentiment. It is a response to something He has done in history. We bless Him because the grave did not hold, and because the One who rose is the same One who spoke the promise. It also rebukes our habit of seeking Him among relics and memories. The living God is to be sought among the living, in His living word and through the Spirit He sent, John 7:39.

crossReferences.note: The first of Jesus' own predictions that He must suffer, be rejected, be killed and be raised on the third day. The angels' 'Remember' in Luke 24:6 to 7 is a direct echo, so the empty tomb is read in the light of a word that the disciples had already heard and not understood.

Jesus takes the Twelve aside and says everything the prophets have written about the Son of Man will be fulfilled, including that on the third day He will rise. Luke adds in 18:34 that they understood none of this. That explains why the angels have to remind the women rather than inform them.

Names Mary Magdalene and Joanna among the women who followed and supported Jesus. When Luke 24:10 names them again, readers know who these women are and that they have been with Jesus from Galilee, which makes them credible witnesses of both the burial and the empty tomb.

The burial account sets up the empty tomb. Joseph lays the body in a tomb where no one had yet been laid, and the women watch where. Because they saw the place, they cannot have gone to the wrong tomb, and the care of the burial scene makes the emptiness a clear fact.

John tells a parallel story of the first morning, with Peter and another disciple running to the tomb and seeing the linen cloths. His fuller account explains Luke's brief verse 12: Peter sees the cloths lying there, and the other disciple 'saw and believed.' The two Gospels fit together as a short and a long telling of the same visit.

Paul's earliest summary of the gospel lists burial, resurrection on the third day 'according to the Scriptures,' and appearances to Cephas, the Twelve and more than five hundred. It covers what Luke 24 is about to narrate and shows the church was reciting the empty tomb and the appearances within a few years of the events.

Peter's Pentecost sermon preaches the resurrection from Psalm 16:10, 'nor will You let Your Holy One see decay,' and says God raised Jesus and that they are all witnesses. It shows the apostles doing, after Pentecost, what the women are told to do here: remember, and tell.

'On the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His presence.' The text speaks of Israel's restoration, and the New Testament does not claim it as a direct prediction of the resurrection. It does supply the pattern of death and raising on the third day that Paul calls 'according to the Scriptures.'

Matthew's account of the same morning has the women meet the risen Jesus, who greets them and says 'Do not be afraid.' It confirms the women's role as first witnesses and shows how differently each Gospel selects, while agreeing that the tomb was empty and the women were sent to tell.

The risen Lord says to John, 'I am the First and the Last, the Living One.' It answers the angels' question in Luke 24:5, 'Why do you look for the living among the dead?' by naming who the Living One is, and adds that He holds the keys of death and Hades.

study.oneStory:
The empty tomb answers a question that runs through the whole Bible: will death have the last word? In Genesis 2:17 and 3:19 death enters as the sentence on Adam, and from Genesis 5 onward the refrain is 'and then he died.' The prophets keep alive a hope that God will swallow up death, Isaiah 25:8, and that His people's dead will live, Daniel 12:2. Israel's own story is told through death and return, from the exile to the valley of dry bones in Ezekiel 37. Luke 24 is where that long hope is finally met.

The passage also settles what the cross meant. On Friday it looked like the end of the story, and the later disciples on the Emmaus road will say so, Luke 24:21. The empty tomb reveals the cross as the way through. The Son of Man 'must be delivered' and 'rise again,' and the second part is as necessary as the first, as the angels say. The promise God made in Genesis 3:15 of a seed who would be wounded and yet crush the serpent begins to be visible in a body that has been in the grave and is now out of it.

It sets up everything after it. The same chapter will bring the risen Lord to meet disciples on the road and in the room, to open the Scriptures, and to commission them. Acts begins with the same claim, and the whole mission of the church is the telling of what the women were first sent to tell. The resurrection is the foundation of preaching, as Paul says, 'if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless,' 1 Corinthians 15:14.

And it points to the end. Paul calls Christ 'the firstfruits,' which means a harvest is coming. The new creation of Revelation 21:4, with 'no more death or mourning or crying or pain,' is the harvest of what began in a garden tomb. Every funeral Christians attend is a funeral held on this side of an empty tomb, and the question 'Why do you look for the living among the dead?' will one day be answered completely, when the last enemy, death, is destroyed, 1 Corinthians 15:26.

quiz.q: What do the women find when they come to the tomb?

options.text: The stone rolled away and the body of the Lord Jesus gone.
options.note: Luke 24:2-3 records the rolled stone and the missing body.

options.text: That the tomb had been disturbed overnight.
options.note: True in a sense, but it misses the specific finding of the empty tomb and absent body.

options.text: The body of Jesus still wrapped inside.
options.note: The body was gone; only the linen cloths remained, as Peter later saw.

options.text: Soldiers still guarding a sealed tomb.
options.note: They found the stone rolled away and the tomb open and empty.

quiz.q: What do the two men in radiant apparel announce?

options.text: He is not here; He has risen, just as He foretold in Galilee.
options.note: Luke 24:6-7 proclaims the resurrection and recalls Jesus' own prediction.

options.text: That Jesus is alive and no longer in the tomb.
options.note: True, but it omits the crucial link to Jesus' own foretelling of His rising.

options.text: That the body had been taken elsewhere.
options.note: The opposite of the angels' message; He has risen, not been relocated.

options.text: That the women should keep the matter secret.
options.note: The women went and reported it; there was no command to stay silent.

quiz.q: Why do the angels tell the women to remember Jesus' words?

options.text: Because the resurrection fulfills exactly what Jesus foretold, so His word interprets the empty tomb.
options.note: Luke 24:6-8 grounds resurrection faith in remembering Jesus' prediction.

options.text: So the women would recall that Jesus had spoken of rising.
options.note: True, but it omits that His word is the key that makes sense of the empty tomb.

options.text: To test whether the women had paid attention.
options.note: The point is not a memory test but that His word explains the event.

options.text: Because the angels had no news of their own to give.
options.note: They proclaim He has risen; recalling His word confirms and interprets it.

quiz.q: How do the apostles first respond to the women's report?

options.text: They dismiss it as nonsense and do not believe, though Peter runs to see the tomb.
options.note: Luke 24:11-12 records the disbelief and Peter's wondering run to the tomb.

options.text: They do not believe the women's account.
options.note: True, but it omits Peter's response of running to the tomb to check.

options.text: They immediately rejoice and believe.
options.note: The opposite; the news seemed like nonsense to them at first.

options.text: They rebuke the women for spreading rumors.
options.note: They disbelieve, but there is no rebuke; Peter goes to investigate.

quiz.q: How does Luke show the resurrection was no accident but God's plan?

options.text: The angels say the Son of Man must be crucified and rise on the third day, a divine necessity Jesus had foretold.
options.note: Luke 24:7 frames the events as a necessity fixed in God's plan and Jesus' word.

options.text: The events happened just as Jesus had predicted.
options.note: True, but it omits the language of necessity, that it must happen.

options.text: The empty tomb surprised even the angels.
options.note: The angels proclaim it confidently as the fulfillment of God's plan.

options.text: The resurrection took God's plan in an unexpected direction.
options.note: It was the appointed path, foretold and necessary, not a detour.

questions: The angels asked, why do you look for the living among the dead? Where are you still seeking life in things that cannot give it, when the risen Christ is alive?
Faith dawned as the women remembered Jesus' words. Which of Christ's promises have you forgotten that would change everything if you truly remembered them?
The resurrection was a divine necessity, foretold in Scripture. How does it steady your faith to know the cross and empty tomb were God's plan all along, not a rescue improvised at the last moment?
The apostles first heard the good news as nonsense. Are there truths about the risen Christ you have half dismissed rather than run, like Peter, to see for yourself?
God entrusted the first news of the resurrection to faithful women the world would discount. Where might God be calling you, ordinary and overlooked, to carry the news that Jesus is alive?

translationNotes.note: 'On the first day of the week' translates a Greek phrase literally reading 'on the first of the Sabbaths', marking the day after the Sabbath. This first day becomes the Lord's Day, the weekly celebration of the resurrection.
'He has risen' renders a passive verb that points to God the Father as the one who raised Jesus. The resurrection is God's act of vindicating His Son, a truth the apostles preach throughout Acts.
The word rendered 'must' expresses divine necessity. The suffering and rising of the Son of Man were fixed in God's saving plan and foretold in Scripture and by Jesus Himself, not a tragic accident.
